3.4 — Projectile Damage, Tuning & Playtest

Your turret shoots, and every bullet passes clean through you. Close that loop — and notice that the bullet is not the thing that does the damage. Then set the numbers that decide whether the fight is tense or unfair.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I make my bullet hurt the player?”Outline only
Break It Down~10 minOutline only

My bullets should actually hurt the player, and the fight should be hard without being unfair.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Give the bullet a name the player can recognisewhat does this part do?Read: 2.1 — Coins: Triggers, Tags & Your First Stat (the tag-and-trigger recipe), and the other.gameObject.CompareTag() row of this lesson's API table
  2. Receive the hit on the object that owns the healthwhat does this part do?Read: the OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other) row of this lesson's API table, and your own 2.1 callback
  3. Spend health through the StatManager you builtwhat does this part do?Read: 2.7 — Refactor Day: Moving Stats into the StatManager
  4. Remove the bullet so one shot costs one hitwhat does this part do?Read: 3.2 — Projectiles: Instantiate(), Fire, Destroy(), and the Destroy(Object obj) row of this lesson's API table

Three of these four parts are lessons you have already finished, and the fourth is the one genuinely new idea: every script you wrote before today changed its own values. A fireball cannot reach the player's health, so the player reaches for the fireball instead — the object that owns the number is the object that reacts, and the bullet only has to be recognisable.

The split is finished when every part names something you could point at in the editor: a tag on a prefab, a branch in a callback, a method on a script, a call. If a part needs the word "and" twice to describe it, it is two parts.

Your turn

Pick two of the parts above and say in one line what each one actually does.

The player's callback does the damage; the fireball itself has no damage code at all. Say who owns the health number, and what the bullet would have to know about the player if it did the work itself.

The E_Fireball branch sits two lines above the Coin branch, in the same callback. What would happen to the player if you merged those two into one if?

In the Editor ~20 min
  1. Project window → Assets/Prefabs/Turret_Projectile, then Inspector → a Circle Collider 2D with Is Trigger ticked, Tag set to E_Fireball, and no Rigidbody 2D. Nothing here needs adding: a trigger needs a body on one of the two objects, and the player has had one since 2.1.
  2. Inspector → Transform → Scale is 4, and the collider's radius is 0.07: the green outline in the Scene view is about 0.28 world units across the art. A collider sized from the import bounds would not match what the player sees.
  3. Edit → Project Settings → Tags and Layers → Tag: confirm E_Fireball exists and note the exact spelling and capitalisation. A tag that does not match is not an error, it is silence — the callback runs and does nothing.
  4. Project window → Assets/Prefabs/Player, then Inspector → the Box Collider 2D, the Rigidbody 2D set to Dynamic, and the Player Controller component. That body is what makes the fireball's trigger fire at all.
  5. Once the code half is done — Game view → press Play and walk into a turret's line of fire: the Console line from ChangeHealth() drops by exactly your number, the fireball vanishes, and at zero your 2.7 Die() runs. Console silent? Check the tag spelling before the code, and the collider before the tag.
  6. Hierarchy → a Turret instance, duplicate it (Ctrl+D) so the Overworld carries three. Give each a different Detection Radius — that collider is per-instance, so three copies of one prefab become three enemies with three reaches. The timing is not per-instance: timeBetweenShots is a field in TurretController.cs, so all three share it until you give it a serialized value.
In the Code ~25 min
APIWhat it isWhat you getWhat it costs
OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other) A callback Unity calls on the object that received the overlap — here, the player. You never call it. The hit report, on the frame the fireball's trigger touches the player's collider. One method has to serve every thing that can touch you — the fireball, the coin, the potion, the enemy. Each one is another branch in the same body.
other.gameObject.CompareTag("E_Fireball") Identity check by tag, on the object that arrived. One check, and you know what hit you. Exact spelling, and the tag must exist. Ask it of other.gameObject — the thing that arrived — never of gameObject, which is you.
manager.ChangeHealth(-2) A public call on the StatManager reference from 2.7. The signed amount that serves damage and healing, with the clamp and the death rule still owned by the stat. Everything public is a promise to every future caller, and the amount is a number written in the player's callback — not a knob anyone can tune without opening the script.
Destroy(other.gameObject) Removes an object at the end of the frame. The cleanup 3.2 used on a lifetime, now on a hit. It has to name other.gameObject. Destroy(gameObject) would delete the player in the middle of a fireball, and nothing would warn you.
E_Fireball A string in Project Settings → Tags and Layers, carried by the prefab. A word the player's callback can test, and the turret's own Enemy tag stays free for 4.6's melee hit. Stringly typed: the compiler cannot check a tag, so a typo compiles and ships.
Architectural specification for the hit.
  • The receiver: which object's script gets the callback, and why is it the player rather than the fireball? The fireball has a collider and no body — what would you have to add before a Turret_Projectile script could receive anything at all? (This is the model the project did not take; be able to say why.)
  • The branch: which tag does your condition test, and which object do you ask? Where does the new branch go relative to the coin, potion and enemy branches that are already in that method?
  • The damage: which method does the branch call, and which sign is the number you pass? Who decides what happens when health reaches zero — the player's branch, or the stat? Say where the clamp lives.
  • The cleanup: which object does the Destroy() call take, and what would Destroy(gameObject) do instead? Does the destroy come before the damage or after it?

Predict Before Building

  1. The player's own callback does the damage, and the fireball carries no damage code at all. Which object owns the health number, and what would the bullet have to know about the player in order to do it itself?
  2. The prefab ships with Is Trigger ticked. Describe what the player feels if you untick it and give the fireball a Dynamic body instead — and name the callback that would have to replace this one.
  3. The fireball is tagged E_Fireball while the turret that fired it is Enemy. Why not reuse Enemy? Say what the player's callback would do in that case that it does not do now.
Playtest ~15 min
  • Swap seats and run a silent playtest, 2.4 rules: you watch, they play, nobody speaks. Did they notice the turret before it fired, or was the first hit a surprise? Did they try to dodge? Then name the number you would move first and where it lives — the Detection Radius (Inspector, per turret), timeBetweenShots (script), Projectile.speed (script), or the damage amount (script, in the player's branch). Change one, play again, and say what the evidence was.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain why the fireball needs no Rigidbody2D, and which object's body makes its trigger fire
  • Explain why the damage happens on the player and not on the bullet, and what other.gameObject means in each line of the branch
  • Say which sign you pass to ChangeHealth(), and who clamps at maxHealth and calls Die()
  • Name the four numbers that decide difficulty, the file or Inspector each lives in, and your value for each
  • Run a silent playtest and make one evidence-based change, then commit and push
